analysis.one_liner: Bans PAC money in House races, limits House campaign spending, and shuts down unregulated party 'soft money'.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 1997, referred to the House Oversight Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten campaign finance rules for House elections. House candidates could no longer take money from political action committees or from anyone outside their own congressional district, and campaigns that accepted voluntary spending limits were capped. It would also have brought unregulated party 'soft money' — big contributions to party committees that dodge federal limits — under federal reporting rules and restrictions, and tightened fundraising rules for federal candidates and officeholders.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, and challengers running against well-funded incumbents. The PAC ban and district-residency rule would force House campaigns to rely on small contributions from the people they would represent, and the soft-money rules would reduce the flow of large, unreported donations through political parties.

how_it_helps.text: House candidates could not accept contributions from multicandidate political committees (PACs) or any source other than individuals [S3].
House candidates could only accept contributions from individual residents of their own congressional district, cutting off money from national donors and PACs [S3].
House candidates who agreed to the rules faced spending and contribution caps of $600,000 per election cycle, with indexing for inflation [S3].

Money solicited, received, or spent by party committees in connection with a federal election would be subject in its entirety to federal contribution limits, prohibitions, and reporting requirements — a direct attack on unregulated 'soft money' [S3].
National party committees would be barred from soliciting or accepting contributions not subject to federal limits, with narrow exceptions [S3].

Federal candidates and officeholders could not raise funds for committees spending outside federal limits, and could not solicit money for tax-exempt groups running voter registration or get-out-the-vote campaigns [S3].
Independent expenditures would be more tightly defined, so coordinated spending could no longer masquerade as 'independent' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees, which would lose House candidates as recipients; national and state party committees, which would lose the soft-money channel; large donors outside a candidate's district, who could no longer give to House races; and incumbents, who would have to raise money under stricter rules and lower limits.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, party committees, and big donors

drawbacks.text: Requiring all contributions to come from a candidate's own district could starve challengers of the national donor networks that incumbents already have, potentially making House seats harder to contest [S3].
The bill partially offsets its restrictions by raising the overall limit on individual contributions by up to $5,000, which benefits large individual donors even as it curbs soft money [S3].

The spending and contribution caps apply only to 'eligible' candidates who agree to them, and the limits lapse entirely if a non-participating opponent exceeds thresholds, so a wealthy self-funder or outside spender could push the field past the caps [S3].

Mandatory contribution bans and limits on political speech raise constitutional questions under the Supreme Court's campaign finance precedents, a challenge any honest supporter would have had to confront [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have meaningfully reduced the role of PAC money and unreported party soft money in House elections, which most reformers viewed as the biggest distortion in the system. The trade-offs are real: the district-residency rule could hurt challengers as much as incumbents, the caps were voluntary and full of escape hatches for opposing spenders, and a higher individual contribution limit was included as a sweetener. On balance it was a genuine reform attempt, though imperfectly designed.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Oversight Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry Costello introduced the bill on January 21, 1997 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Oversight [S5].
No other action was ever taken on the bill for the rest of the 105th Congress [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, PACs, party committees, and large donors kept the existing system — unlimited soft money to parties and PAC money in House races. Incumbent lawmakers faced no new fundraising restrictions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs, party committees, and big donors

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its single sponsor was a Democrat and it drew zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: PACs would be barred outright from contributing to House candidates, ending their direct channel to lawmakers. PAC money is concentrated organizational money, not voter money.

Parties would lose the soft-money channel — large contributions outside federal limits — and face caps on party election spending and stricter reporting. This was the main source of unregulated money in federal campaigns at the time.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and out-of-district contributors
industries.note: They could no longer give to House candidates outside their own district, but the bill raised the overall individual contribution limit by up to $5,000.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and congressional candidates
industries.note: Federal candidates and officeholders would face new restrictions on fundraising for parties, other candidates, and tax-exempt groups, and House campaigns would face caps — though the caps were voluntary with exemptions when opponents outspent them.
